**Record of the Royal Charter Commission Text**

The text describes an official inquiry into the wreck of the Royal Charter, a steam clipper ship. A commission was appointed to investigate the loss, and it held its sittings at Liverpool, beginning on 6 February 1860. The proceedings were conducted before Mr. Tremenheere, who was assisted by Captains Harris and Gray, both of the Board of Trade.

The vessel itself was of 2,719 tons register and had been built on the Clyde at Sandycroft in 1855. On her final voyage she departed Melbourne on 26 August 1859 carrying 388 passengers and a crew of 112. Her general cargo included 79,000 ounces of gold, packed in 39 boxes and consigned to banks in London. The ship was under the command of Captain John Taylor, who had sailed with her since her very first voyage.

The crossing to Britain took fifty-nine days and was made against heavy westerly winds. On the morning of 25 October, the ship rounded the Mull of Galloway and took two pilots aboard at Point Lynas. That same evening, the wind backed round to the northeast, and by ten o'clock it had increased to hurricane force. Although the ship's engines, rated at 200 nominal horsepower, were worked to their utmost, she drifted stern-first toward the coast of Anglesey. At half past one in the morning of 26 October, she struck the rocks half a mile east of Moelfre.

The account then details the rescue efforts. The first boat launched was stove in against the ship's side. A raft constructed by the carpenter, Peter Gibson, succeeded in carrying the purser and twenty men to shore, and a buoy line rigged by the mate, Joseph Rodgers, saved a further nineteen people. In total, 41 persons survived out of the 500 aboard. As for the gold, all but one of the consignments went down with the ship; a single box containing 1,640 ounces was recovered from the beach at Moelfre in November by a local man named Robert Williams.

Finally, the text sets out the commission's findings and recommendations. The commission concluded that the ship had been seaworthy and well found. It further found that the pilots had advised standing out to sea when the wind shifted, and that the decision to anchor in Moelfre roads had been taken by Captain Taylor against that advice. The commissioners recommended the establishment of a storm signal station at Point Lynas and a lifeboat at Moelfre, and both of these recommendations were carried out within two years by the Marine Board.

# Record of the Submarine Telegraph Company's Annual Report, 1868

The Submarine Telegraph Company produced its annual report covering the year that ended on 31 December 1868. This report was presented to the shareholders at a general meeting, which took place at the company's offices in Lothbury, London, on 11 February 1869. The meeting was chaired by the company's president, Sir Charles Bright.

The report set out the state of the company's operations. It disclosed that the company was then operating 1,940 nautical miles of submarine cable. Of this total, 310 miles had been laid during the year just ended, at a cost of 118,000 pounds. This new mileage consisted of two works: a new circuit running from Dover to Cape Grisnez, measuring 26 miles, and an extension from Cromer to Hanstholm, measuring 284 miles.

On the financial side, the report showed that the company's gross receipts for the year amounted to 147,300 pounds. This represented an increase of 11,200 pounds compared with the receipts of 1867.
